{"id": "2:265/q07", "question": "Is the image read as a garden or a grain?", "turns_on": "A reported alternative word in the comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q07/p1", "position": "جنة, a garden.", "reasons": "The standard wording is retained by the sources recording the variant. {"id": "2:265/q08", "question": "What does ربوة mean?", "turns_on": "Whether rabā denotes geographical elevation, soil's swelling growth, or a low place.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q08/p1", "position": "Raised ground, often level and fertile, above its surroundings or runoff.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Hasan stress level elevation; Ibn Abbas and Dahhak say rivers do not flow through this garden, though al-Qurtubi notes hills may have water. Al-Yazidi specifies above the watercourse. The root rabā means rise or increase; al-A'sha's poem depicts upland gardens. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi limit the no-rivers detail to this rain-fed setting. Al-Damghani allows level raised ground or a hill and also points to 23:50; Jishumi says the word has seven dialectal forms and attributes the elevation gloss to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Rabi'."}, {"id": "2:265/q08/p2", "position": "Fertile soil that swells and rises after rain, rather than an ordinary hill.", "reasons": "Razi cites 22:5 and the contrast with sterile stone, objecting that hills lack streams and face wind while hollows flood. Bursevi and Study Quran repeat the growth argument."}, {"id": "2:265/q08/p3", "position": "A low place.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi's rabāwa is transmitted by Ibn Atiyya and others; Ibn Atiyya calls it awkward, and al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin reject it because the root denotes increase and height."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q09", "question": "How is ربوة read?", "turns_on": "Dialectal vowel and added-alif forms, with preference based on prevalence and plural morphology.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q09/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on rāʾ, rubwa.", "reasons": "Widely attributed to the Hijaz, Medina and Iraq; Abu Hatim, Abu Ubayd, Abu al-Hasan, al-Akhfash, al-Tabari and al-Tabrisi prefer it as common or because the plural rubā/rubā supports it. The same variation occurs in 23:50. Jishumi calls the damma form the more common Qurashi form and says the variation also occurs in 23:50. Al-Nashr specifies that all readers other than Ibn Amir and Asim use ḍamma on the rāʾ in both al-Baqara and al-Mu'minun (23:50)."}, {"id": "2:265/q09/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on rāʾ, rabwa.", "reasons": "Attributed to Asim and Ibn Amir and to Tamim; Ibn Khalawayh calls both principal forms eloquent dialects. Jishumi attributes this form to Asim and Ibn Amir in 23:50 as well."}, {"id": "2:265/q09/p3", "position": "With kasra on rāʾ, ribwa.", "reasons": "Reported from Ibn Abbas and also Hasan, al-A'mash and Abu Ishaq; al-Tabari rejects it as a recitation. Jishumi transmits the kasra form from Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "2:265/q09/p4", "position": "Rabāwa with an added alif and fatḥa.", "reasons": "Attributed to Abu Ja'far, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Ibn Abbas and Abu Razin, with variants reported in 23:50."}, {"id": "2:265/q09/p5", "position": "Rabāwa with added alif and kasra.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Ashhab al-Uqayli; reports vary in spelling. Jishumi also transmits a ribawa form with kasra and added alif."}, {"id": "2:265/q09/p6", "position": "A lengthened form with ḍamma.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this to Ubayy and Asim al-Jahdari."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q10", "question": "Why is the garden placed on a rabwa, and what setting is envisaged?", "turns_on": "Elevation and water's agricultural effects, and whether a named region is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q10/p1", "position": "Raised, fertile ground produces especially fine, abundant fruit.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari invokes richer soil and al-A'sha's upland verse. Al-Biqa'i cites sun and pollinating winds; Bursevi and Alusi cite mild, unstagnant air; al-Baydawi cites cool air. Ibn Atiyya rejects identifying Riyad al-Hazn as the precise setting, explaining Najd and Tihama differ; Abu Hayyan follows. Ibn Qutayba says orchards are generally best on heights; Jishumi describes a high, level site where streams run without flooding it and growth is greater."}, {"id": "2:265/q10/p2", "position": "The image is the rain-fed, raised garden familiar in Arabia, with no stream in this instance.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya confines Ibn Abbas's no-rivers description to this garden, citing another raised place with a spring in 23:50; al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan agree the word need not exclude water universally."}, {"id": "2:265/q10/p3", "position": "The fertile raised garden may have flowing water.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi describe level raised land supplied by water; Ibn Kathir reports streams in Ibn Abbas's and Dahhak's descriptions, while al-Qurtubi says a rabwa can have water. Jishumi describes streams running through the high, level site without inundating it."}, {"id": "2:265/q10/p4", "position": "The parable's land is Egypt.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam says dew supports Egyptian soil and heavy rain doubles its yield. Al-Tha'labi's report instead says rain weakens it, a conflicting detail preserved here."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q11", "question": "What does وابل mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q11/p1", "position": "A heavy, abundant downpour.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives paired Arabic verb forms for raining and the adjective mobūla; al-Mawardi cites Adi ibn Zayd's verse; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi describe intense rain."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q12", "question": "What is the syntax of أصابها وابل?", "turns_on": "Whether the rain clause is descriptive or circumstantial, and whether its antecedent is garden or ground.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q12/p1", "position": "It is a second adjective describing the garden.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin put lasting location before temporary rainfall; al-Qurtubi says the pronoun points to the raised tract."}, {"id": "2:265/q12/p2", "position": "It describes the rabwa, of which the garden is part.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa gives this alternative; al-Qurtubi takes the pronoun as the elevated ground."}, {"id": "2:265/q12/p3", "position": "It is circumstantial from the garden or the pronoun within its location phrase.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan allows a circumstantial clause; al-Samin specifies either the implicit pronoun or the now specified garden, with qad understood in the latter."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q13", "question": "What does آتت أكلها mean and how is آتت construed?", "turns_on": "Whether آتت retains 'gave' with an omitted recipient or means 'produced' with one object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q13/p1", "position": "The garden gives its edible produce, with an implicit owner or people as first object and أكلها as second.", "reasons": "Al-Samin prefers the ordinary two-object construction and calls the giving metaphorical; Abu Hayyan supplies owner or people. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say the possessive is association, not garden ownership."}, {"id": "2:265/q13/p2", "position": "آتت means produced or brought forth, taking أكلها as its sole object.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa offers this and Bursevi permits it; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin's al-Shaykh object that Arabic does not attest this meaning of آتت."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q14", "question": "What does أكلها mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q14/p1", "position": "Its edible fruit, crop, food or produce.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, al-Tabari and Abu al-Hasan distinguish food from the act of eating; the poet's meal/hunger line and 14:25 support edible produce. {"id": "2:265/q15", "question": "How is أكلها read?", "turns_on": "Pronunciation with or without the medial vowel; meaning remains produce.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q15/p1", "position": "The light form has sukūn on kāf in the feminine possessive.", "reasons": "Attributed to Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Abu Amr. {"id": "2:265/q16", "question": "How much and how often does ضعفين signify?", "turns_on": "Whether the dual counts amount, harvests, or repeated multiplication, and the baseline to which a double is compared.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q16/p1", "position": "Twice the ordinary or comparable garden's crop.", "reasons": "Most interpreters count an amount plus its equal; Ata and Ibn Abbas compare one year here with two elsewhere. Al-Qurtubi prefers twice the fruit of other land over two yearly harvests. The cause is the high ground plus heavy rain. Jishumi reports al-Zajjaj's account of a double as the original amount plus an addition; Abu Muslim compares the crop to this garden's customary yield, while al-Asamm and Abu Ali compare other gardens."}, {"id": "2:265/q16/p2", "position": "Two harvests in one year.", "reasons": "Ikrima reports two fruitings; al-Tabrisi specifies six months apart and cites 14:25. Al-Qurtubi prefers a quantity comparison instead."}, {"id": "2:265/q16/p3", "position": "Four times the ordinary crop.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i prefers this: each double is original plus its equal, so two doubles are four. Al-Tabrisi, al-Baydawi, Bursevi and others transmit the reckoning."}, {"id": "2:265/q16/p4", "position": "Three times the ordinary crop.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim is reported by Abu Hayyan; Taj al-Qurra rejects it as unsupported in Arabic."}, {"id": "2:265/q16/p5", "position": "Repeated or manyfold abundance, without an exact count.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan favors repeated multiples to match multiplied good deeds; Ibn Ashur compares the dual to labbayk. Al-Alusi reports this reading."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q17", "question": "What grammatical role does ضعفين have?", "turns_on": "Whether آتت has an omitted recipient and the doubled amount is a state, or the doubled amount is made its object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q17/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative describing the crop as multiplied.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi and al-Baydawi parse it this way; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin reject treating it as a second object of آتت."}, {"id": "2:265/q17/p2", "position": "It is the second object of آتت.", "reasons": "Reported as a proposal only; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call it erroneous because the garden's produce is already the object."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q18", "question": "What does طل mean?", "turns_on": "Literal fine rain versus a reported figurative extension to dew.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q18/p1", "position": "Light, fine drizzle or gentle rain.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj describes persistent fine rain scarcely making runoff; al-Wahidi gives small drops and related forms; Juwair calls it rakk. Ibn Atiyya calls this common Arabic usage; al-Tabrisi records other lexical uses related to moisture. Al-Biqa'i describes dew as an early stage of rainfall. Jishumi contrasts tall's fine droplets with the larger, forceful drops of wabil and attributes gentle rain to al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' and Qatada."}, {"id": "2:265/q18/p2", "position": "Dew or nighttime moisture on plants.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others report dew; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call this figurative compared with fine rain. Al-Qummi specifies nighttime dew. Jishumi attributes the dew gloss to al-Suddi."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q19", "question": "How does فإن لم يصبها وابل فطل work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Which constituent is omitted after the conditional, and whether any inversion is necessary.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q19/p1", "position": "An omitted verb or predicate completes the condition: if no downpour strikes, drizzle does or suffices.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and al-Tabari supply kāna or a prior event and cite a poem; al-Wahidi compares a one-or-two-slave example. Al-Mubarrad supplies 'rain is enough'; al-Zajjaj says 'what reaches it is light rain.' Abu Hayyan and al-Samin set out subject/predicate and omitted-verb parses, with Imru al-Qays's line as parallel. Jishumi explicitly supplies an omitted kana to account for the past-tense conditional and compares a manumission example; al-Farra's heading likewise identifies the elision."}, {"id": "2:265/q19/p2", "position": "The order is inverted, so yielding follows either downpour or drizzle.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report and reject this as unnecessary; ordinary order already conveys the sense."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q20", "question": "What happens if only طل reaches the garden?", "turns_on": "Whether light moisture preserves the same multiplied crop or produces a smaller yet reliable one.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q20/p1", "position": "The fertile garden still gives a full or doubled yield; little moisture suffices.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf invokes fertile soil; al-Baghawi says steady light dew can do a downpour's work. Razi and Abu Hayyan offer full-yield possibilities; al-Wahidi and al-Nasafi say the crop remains abundant. Ibn Qutayba expressly says lighter rain does not diminish its yield compared with heavy rain."}, {"id": "2:265/q20/p2", "position": "The garden yields less than under heavy rain, but still yields something beneficial.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi argues dew-fed crops are weaker than rain-fed crops; Razi allows this alternative; Ibn Ashur links varying yield to varying sincerity."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q21", "question": "What does the orchard teach about sincere giving?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q21/p1", "position": "Sincere charity or a believer's deed remains fruitful and multiplied, whether the gift is large or small.", "reasons": "Qatada says God's promise never fails; al-Suddi connects doubled fruit to doubled reward. Al-Mawardi urges giving even a little. Razi, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur say degree depends on sincerity, effort, attachment to wealth, recipient need and accompanying circumstances. Al-Qummi's lawful-date report and al-Qurtubi's Abu Hurayra report depict God nurturing a date to mountain size. Jishumi cites al-Hasan and Qatada: God multiplies small and large gifts and never withholds their recompense; he says the promise encourages charity."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q22", "question": "What does God's seeing deeds convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q22/p1", "position": "God knows outward deeds and inward motives, records and recompenses them; the close promises reward and warns against display.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari distinguishes sincere from hurtful giving and warns against neglected obligations; Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and others see both promise and warning. Razi notes amount and manner; al-Biqa'i urges improvement of inward and outward work. Al-Khattabi says basir's form functions as an active participle. Jishumi says God rewards each according to spending and intention, and reports Abu Muslim's distinction between ostentation and sincerity."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q23", "question": "How is تعملون read, and whom does it address?", "turns_on": "A change in grammatical person and the antecedent of the third-person pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q23/p1", "position": "Second-person تعملون addresses the audience directly.", "reasons": "The majority reading shifts from third-person narration to direct address, making God's knowledge a promise and warning."}, {"id": "2:265/q23/p2", "position": "Third-person يعملون refers to all people or specifically the donors; one report also relates it to hypocrites.", "reasons": "Al-Zuhri is named for the variant. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say a donor-only reference makes it pure promise; Abu Hayyan also mentions hypocrites."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q24", "question": "How does the verse connect with the surrounding spending parables and passage?", "turns_on": "Which earlier image supplies the main comparison: the barren rock or the multiplying seed.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q24/p1", "position": "It contrasts accepted, fertile giving with showy or harmful giving that the preceding rock image leaves barren.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan contrast 2:264; Ibn Ashur says contrast clarifies rank and renews praise. Al-Tabataba'i treats the linked verses as a unit addressing purpose, manner, good wealth, needy recipients and reward. Jishumi contrasts the two traits of sound charity with the two faults of reminder and harm in 2:264, reporting the Qadi's formulation."}, {"id": "2:265/q24/p2", "position": "It develops the earlier seed image: the lasting orchard pictures sustained generosity and further multiplication.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the grain represents spending in God's path while the orchard covers every good path. Ibn Ashur says the simpler seed image quickly pictures multiplication; this one has several favorable features. Elmalili says double does not reduce the earlier seven-hundredfold promise."}]}

{"id": "2:265/q26", "question": "What reports about charity's effects are cited with this verse?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted statements about charity's effect.", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q26/p1", "position": "A lawfully earned date given in charity is nurtured by God until it becomes mountain-sized.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites Abu Hurayra's Prophetic report through Muslim and the Muwatta; Study Quran also invokes it."}, {"id": "2:265/q26/p2", "position": "Charity itself speaks of five benefits: growth, enlargement, turning an enemy friendly, preservation and protection.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits the report through Ali from the Prophet."}, {"id": "2:265/q26/p3", "position": "Hell prostrates in gratitude when a believer gives charity, because it frees someone from punishment.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports Makhul's saying."}]}

{"id": "2:265/q29", "question": "What do ابتغاء and مرضات mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q29/p1", "position": "ابتغاء means seeking, and مرضات names satisfaction or approval.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi derives marḍāt as the verbal noun of raḍiya. {"id": "2:265/q30", "question": "What verbal sense underlies تثبيتا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q30/p1", "position": "Causative ثبّت means to make firm or establish, distinct from intransitive ثبت, to become firm.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin's al-Shaykh insist on this distinction, opposing replacement by the intransitive verbal noun unless a licensing verb precedes it. {"id": "2:265/q31", "question": "How are جنة and ربوة pronounced when pausing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q31/p1", "position": "Their feminine tāʾ is pronounced hāʾ at pause according to written form and practice.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr states the pause rule for singular feminine nouns without open ta, using janna bi-rabwa as an example; it also contrasts indefinite nonfeminine accusatives and rejects Ibn Jabbara's alleged hāʾ stops at other words as contrary to the script and performance practice."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q32", "question": "How should ربوة be classified when distinguishing a word's forms and meanings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q32/p1", "position": "Its occurrence should not be inflated into a distinct sense of riba merely because the forms are related.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi rejects a grouping that makes the garden-on-a-height expression a separate riba sense. {"id": "2:265/q34", "question": "What reports about prayer and recitation occur alongside the discussion of rain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q34/p1", "position": "Al-Nashr recounts supplication in drought and other prayer reports, while rejecting a report about prayer upon completing the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr relates Abu Sulayman's resolve to pray with both hands extended, a report through Abu Awana of the Prophet directing people to kneel and invoke God during drought before rain came, a prayer in Muslim asking forgiveness and good character, and its author's rejection of a report of the Prophet standing to supplicate at Qur'an completion."}]}
{"id": "2:265/q35", "question": "How do modern discussions explain the guiding purpose of scriptural parables and stories?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:265/q35/p1", "position": "Their intended lesson can be moral guidance and reflection, with later writers debating the relation of that lesson to historical detail.", "reasons": "Rifai reports Taha Husayn's caution about historical inference from shared names; Abduh's account of Qur'anic stories as admonition rather than detailed chronicle; Khalaf Allah's symbolic account likened to parables and the criticism it received; and Iqbal's symbolic reading of Adam. {"id": "2:266/q09", "question": "What does the phrase about rivers beneath the garden describe?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of the pronoun and the syntactic role of the river clause.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q09/p1", "position": "It describes the garden, with beneath referring to its trees.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explicitly identifies the trees. {"id": "2:266/q12", "question": "How is min kull al-thamarat construed?", "turns_on": "Whether min is licensed as an extra particle and whether all implies literal totality.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q12/p1", "position": "An omitted noun such as provision, fruit or food is understood before the prepositional phrase.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan rejects extra min under Kufan and standard Basran conditions and supplies rizq or thamarat; al-Samin supplies rizq or fakiha, citing al-Nabigha and 37:164; Bursavi compares 37:164. {"id": "2:266/q13", "question": "How does the past wording for old age fit the wish construction?", "turns_on": "Whether waw is circumstantial, or the past clause follows an implied law or the sense of the wish.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q13/p1", "position": "The waw introduces a circumstantial clause, with qad understood, describing the owner when he has the garden.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi give or permit this analysis. {"id": "2:266/q19", "question": "What is an i'sar?", "turns_on": "Whether the word itself is a general rotating wind, a hot samum, or a cold blast.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q19/p1", "position": "A fierce, rotating wind or whirlwind rising like a column, often lifting dust.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari gives its plural a'asir and cites Yazid ibn Mufarrigh; al-Zajjaj calls it zawba'a and cites an unnamed poet. Al-Thalabi cites al-Kumayt and Yazid ibn al-Muqri; Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Tabrisi, al-Samin and Ibn Abbas in al-Durr cite poetry or the wind proverb. Al-Jawhari adds umm zawba'a and says the name also belongs to a jinn chief. Al-Alusi describes colliding air currents, possible upward or downward motion and force enough to uproot trees or snatch boats. Al-Tabatabai describes a twisting dust column between earth and sky. Damghani says the fierce wind can be cold or hot. Jishumi describes its column rising from ground to sky, or a wind that raises clouds. Al-Itqan cites an anonymous poetic line and gives the singular-plural pair isar/aasir. Bint al-Shati cites Ibn Abbas's fierce-wind gloss and poem, al-Jawhari's dust-pillar or thundercloud, al-Tabari's comparable gloss and al-Raghib's dust-stirring wind; she finds the severe-wind reading suited to the root."}, {"id": "2:266/q19/p2", "position": "It is specifically the deadly hot wind called samum.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi gives this gloss through al-Mawardi; Ibn Atiyya calls the whirlwind violent and scorching. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi in al-Qurtubi describe the hot wind. Ibn Ashur identifies a violent hot wind likened to fire or samum. Bint al-Shati reports al-Tabari's transmission from Ibn Abbas that the fierce wind carries scorching heat, including samum."}, {"id": "2:266/q19/p3", "position": "It is a cold blast or frost.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan gives this second gloss in Ibn Abi Hatim; al-Hasan and al-Dahhak elsewhere describe cold within the whirlwind."}]}
{"id": "2:266/q20", "question": "Why is the whirlwind called i'sar?", "turns_on": "Which observed squeezing or twisting motivates the word; Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi disagree about the cloth derivation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q20/p1", "position": "Its coiling motion resembles cloth being wrung.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi cites a poem; al-Mahdawi gives the derivation in Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. {"id": "2:266/q21", "question": "What is the fire in the whirlwind?", "turns_on": "Whether the destructive fire is heat, cold, actual flame, lightning, or Hell's breath.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q21/p1", "position": "Scorching samum or exceptionally hot wind.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas repeatedly calls it samum; Qatada calls the wind a carrier of it and al-Suddi distinguishes wind from its fire. {"id": "2:266/q23", "question": "What do the successive fa and burning verb convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q23/p1", "position": "The storm strikes after the garden has become useful, then the garden burns up as the intransitive result of burning it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reads the successive fa as sequence after ripening; he and al-Samin distinguish intransitive ihtaraqa from transitive ahraqa. {"id": "2:266/q25", "question": "What reflection does the closing appeal seek?", "turns_on": "Which lesson of the parable the reflective command highlights.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q25/p1", "position": "Understand the parables, take warning or guidance, and act or obey accordingly.", "reasons": "Mujahid glosses reflection as obedience; Qatada cites 29:43 that the learned understand parables. {"id": "2:266/q27", "question": "What does the ruined garden represent?", "turns_on": "The context of spending, the scope of the image, and whether ruin comes from insincere giving, harm, later sin, neglected obedience or unbelief.", "positions": [{"id": "2:266/q27/p1", "position": "Showy or insincere charity, whose apparent reward vanishes at Judgment when needed most.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi repeatedly identifies another parable for ostentatious spending.
